Series::LinearAlgAccessor::svd¶

Back to Series::LinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

SvdDecomposition Series::LinearAlgAccessor::svd(bool full_matrices = true) const
SvdDecomposition SeriesLinearAlgProxy::svd(bool full_matrices = true) const

What It Does¶

svd() returns the three coordinated factors in

A = U diag(S) Vh

The returned SvdDecomposition has three public Series fields:

  • .u: orthonormal directions in the output space

  • .s: nonnegative strengths, ordered largest to smallest

  • .vh: orthonormal input directions, stored as rows

Use this joint method when the factors must be used together: reconstruction, low-rank approximation, basis conversion, or an algorithm that needs both directions and strengths. Use svd_u(), svd_s(), or svd_vh() when the code consumes only one component and returning a decomposition object would obscure that intent.

Calling Styles And The Two Signature Types¶

The two signatures do not perform different decompositions. They describe two ways the accessor machinery reaches the same unary operation:

auto direct = matrix.linearalg.svd(false);    // Series::LinearAlgAccessor
auto proxied = matrix.linearalg().svd(false); // SeriesLinearAlgProxy

matrix.linearalg is the accessor stored on matrix. Calling linearalg() creates a lightweight proxy bound to that same matrix. Because SVD is unary, the proxy does not need a peer and both expressions decompose matrix with the same full_matrices setting. Users normally write the shorter direct form.

The peer-bound form matrix.linearalg(other) exists for binary methods such as matmul() and lu_solve(). Do not bind an unrelated peer for svd(); SVD has only one numeric input.

Rotation, Scaling, Rotation¶

Read the factorization from right to left. Vh first expresses an input in principal input directions. diag(S) independently scales those coordinates. U then expresses the scaled result in output coordinates.

A singular value near zero identifies a direction almost erased by the map. Exactly zero means rank deficiency: different inputs can produce the same output. The ratio between the largest and smallest retained singular values describes how strongly reversing the map can amplify error.

Parameter¶

full_matrices (bool, default true) Controls whether U and Vh include complete orthonormal bases or only the directions needed to reconstruct A. It never changes .s.

For input [...,m,n], let k=min(m,n):

mode

.u

.s

.vh

true

[...,m,m]

[...,k]

[...,n,n]

false

[...,m,k]

[...,k]

[...,k,n]

Reduced mode is usually the practical choice: it reconstructs the complete input with fewer stored values and is the mode supported by reverse mode. Full mode is useful when an algorithm explicitly needs bases for left or right null-space complements.

Returns¶

SvdDecomposition A value object containing coordinated .u, .s, and .vh fields. It is not itself a Series; select a field before applying Series methods.

Gradient¶

Reverse mode is supported with full_matrices=false. A loss may depend on one or several returned fields, and sensitivities propagate to the original matrix.

Singular-vector derivatives require distinct singular values. When two values are equal, their shared subspace is defined but no unique pair of basis vectors is. Near equality therefore makes gradients through .u or .vh unstable. Objectives that depend only symmetrically on .s are generally better behaved.

Examples¶

Example 1. Direct-accessor and unary-proxy calls are equivalent.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
auto direct = matrix.linearalg.svd(false);
auto proxied = matrix.linearalg().svd(false);

std::cout << "direct_s=" << direct.s << "\n";
std::cout << "proxy_s=" << proxied.s << "\n";

Output¶

direct_s=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 2]
proxy_s=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 2]

The class names in the signatures explain routing; they are not two algorithms the caller must choose between.

Example 2. Reconstruct a coupled matrix from reduced factors.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
auto parts = matrix.linearalg.svd(false);
auto scale = parts.s.diag_embed();
auto reconstructed = parts.u.linearalg.mm(scale).linearalg.mm(parts.vh);

std::cout << reconstructed << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[3, 1],
  [1, 3]]

diag_embed() turns the singular-value vector into the middle k x k scale matrix. This multiplication is the operational meaning of the factorization.

Example 3. The singular directions are orthonormal.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}});
auto parts = matrix.linearalg.svd(false);

std::cout << "u=" << parts.u.transpose(0, 1).linearalg.mm(parts.u) << "\n";
std::cout << "vh=" << parts.vh.linearalg.mm(parts.vh.transpose(0, 1)) << "\n";

Output¶

u=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 1.9967346e-16],
  [1.9967346e-16, 1]]
vh=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 4.2664216e-17],
  [4.2664216e-17, 1]]

The tiny off-diagonal values are floating-point roundoff. Orthogonality and reconstruction are reliable validation criteria; exact vector signs are not.

Example 4. On a tall 3 x 2 matrix, reduced and full mode differ in U.

auto tall = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 2.0}, {0.0, 0.0}});
auto reduced = tall.linearalg.svd(false);
auto full = tall.linearalg.svd(true);

std::cout << "reduced_u=" << reduced.u << "\n";
std::cout << "full_u=" << full.u << "\n";
std::cout << "s=" << reduced.s << "\n";

Output¶

reduced_u=pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 0],
  [0, 1],
  [0, 0]]
full_u=pluss::Series(shape=[3,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=9, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 0, 0],
  [0, 1, 0],
  [0, 0, 1]]
s=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 2]

The extra full-mode column spans an output direction not reached by this map.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Input must have at least two dimensions; the last two are matrix dimensions.

  • Leading dimensions are batches and are decomposed independently.

  • Singular-vector signs are arbitrary. Paired sign changes in U and Vh leave reconstruction unchanged.

  • Repeated singular values make individual singular vectors non-unique.

  • Full factors consume more memory and are not supported by reverse mode.

  • SvdDecomposition is a three-field result, not a Series.

Summary¶

Use svd(false) when an algorithm needs coordinated reduced factors. Read .vh as input directions, .s as their strengths, and .u as the resulting output directions. Use full mode only when complete null-space bases are part of the task.

See Also¶

  • svd_u: return only output-space directions.

  • svd_s: return only ordered singular strengths.

  • svd_vh: return only input-space directions.

  • pinverse: reverse directions whose singular values survive a cutoff.
